newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK jobless queues to shrink again in Jan.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK jobless queues to shrink again in Jan.

text.p: Britain's jobless queues are expected to have shortened again in January as the rapid rate of decline in unemployment continued, economists said on Monday.

Figures for unemployment, average earnings and unit wage costs will be released at 0930 GMT on Wednesday. A Reuter poll of economists forecast a 30,000 fall in unemployment in the first month of the year.
A net 45,000 people were taken off the unemployment registers in December following a staggering 96,000 drop the month before.

But part of that was due to distortions from the jobseekers allowance, a new scheme to replace old-style unemployment benefit. The introduction of the allowance led to a backlog of claims and exaggerated the scale of recent jobless falls, the Office for National Statistics said.
But economists are uncertain whether that effect will persist into 1997.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, said the JSA would continue to overstate the drop in unemployment over the next few months.
"But in January, this effect may be offset by adverse seasonal effects from heavy snow," he said, forecasting a 20,000 fall in the January jobless total.
Marian Bell, economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland, pencilled in a 25,000 drop and said the JSA effect should have begun to unwind in January.
"This month, we would expect any further distortion to the figures to be minor and for the fall in unemployment to return to more trend levels," she said.
The main concern that rapidly falling unemployment raises for the financial markets is that a dearth of available workers will force wage levels higher.
For that reason, the average earnings figures will be just as closely scrutinised as the headline unemployment number.

The Reuter poll showed annualised average earnings growth is forecast to have held steady at 4.0 percent in December while unit wage costs eased to 3.6 percent in the three months to December compared with the same period a year earlier.
"The big risk to UK inflation is the labour market and wages," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economist at BankAmerica.

He said there was a significant risk that rapidly falling unemployment will force up wages. "If that happens, it will be virtually impossible to keep inflation in check without a rate hike. This makes Wednesday's labour market report almost more important than the RPIs themselves."
Retail price index (RPI) figures for January are due out on Thursday.
The consensus forecast for an unchanged rate of earnings growth will ease fears of a building wage-price spiral. But Bell expects a pick-up to 4.25 percent.
"It has been reported that shortages of skilled labour are leading companies to increase wages in order to retain current members of staff," she said.
That trend will increase the further unemployment falls.

Saunders said survey evidence indicated a slight rise in the median level of wage settlements and added that hefty bonuses paid out in the financial services and banking sector would put upward pressure on overall average earnings.
"But on balance, we doubt that these effects will be strong enough to cause earnings growth to take a step up."
